title: The night Los Angeles fired at an enemy that never came
hook: Los Angeles fired over a thousand shells at an enemy that never came.
summary: In February 1942, days after a Japanese submarine shelled California, Los Angeles blacked out and fired about 1,400 anti-aircraft shells at unidentified objects; no enemy planes were found, yet five people died.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Los Angeles: air raid alert on 24-25 February 1942, about 1,430 anti-aircraft shells fired, five civilian deaths, Navy Secretary Knox called it a false alarm
Wikipedia, Bombardment of Ellwood: Japanese submarine I-17 shelled an oil field near Santa Barbara on 23 February 1942
U.S. Army Center of Military History / Office of Air Force History account of the 1942 Los Angeles air raid

lines.text: Los Angeles fired over one thousand shells at an enemy that never came.
lines.caps: *Los Angeles | fired over *1,000 | shells at an *enemy

lines.text: It was February nineteen forty-two, weeks after Pearl Harbor.
A Japanese submarine had just shelled an oil field nearby.
So when radar spotted something unknown, sirens wailed and the city went dark.
Searchlights swept the sky while guns fired at shapes nobody could name.

image.search: Battle of Los Angeles 1942 searchlights photograph

lines.text: No enemy plane was ever found.
But falling shells killed three people, and two more died of heart attacks.
lines.caps: But falling *shells | killed *three people, | two more *heart attacks

lines.text: The Navy called it a false alarm.

post.caption:
In 1942, a whole city fought a battle against nothing. To this day, nobody agrees on what the searchlights chased.
Would you have believed it was a real attack?
Follow @unt.oldfiles for a new untold story every day.
